title: The Layers of the Atmosphere
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: The atmosphere is the blanket of gases that surrounds the Earth and makes life possible. It supplies the oxygen that animals breathe, the carbon dioxide that plants need, and the water that falls as rain. It also protects the planet from the worst of the sun's radiation and from most of the small rocks that fall from space, which burn up as shooting stars. Air has no clear upper edge, but fades gradually into space, and scientists divide it into five layers according to changes in temperature. This passage describes the layers in order, starting at the ground and ending at the edge of space.

The lowest layer is the troposphere, which extends from the ground to a height of between eight and fifteen kilometres, depending on the place and the season. It is the thinnest layer but contains about three quarters of the mass of the air, and almost all of the water vapour, which is why all weather occurs here. Temperature falls with height, by roughly six degrees for every thousand metres, so the top of the troposphere is bitterly cold, at about minus fifty degrees. Aeroplanes fly near the top of this layer, where the air is thin and smooth, and where they can travel faster using less fuel.

Above it lies the stratosphere, which reaches to about fifty kilometres. Here the temperature rises with height, because the layer contains the ozone layer, a thin region of gas that absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation from the sun and turns it into heat. Without the ozone, life on land would be impossible. The air in the stratosphere is calm and dry, with no storms, and the clouds are rare. Weather balloons can rise into it, and so do a few very high aircraft, but ordinary passengers never see it. In the 1980s, scientists discovered a hole in the ozone layer above Antarctica, which led the world's governments to ban the chemicals responsible.

The mesosphere extends from about fifty to eighty-five kilometres above the ground. It is the coldest layer, with temperatures as low as minus ninety degrees, and the air is so thin that it is almost impossible to measure from the ground. Most meteors burn up here, as the friction of the air heats them, which is why we see shooting stars in the night sky. Because the mesosphere is too high for balloons and too low for satellites, it remains the least understood layer, and scientists must study it using rockets, which spend only a few minutes passing through it.

Next comes the thermosphere, which reaches to about six hundred kilometres. The temperature here may exceed a thousand degrees, but a person would not feel hot, because the air is so thin that there are too few particles to transfer the heat. The thermosphere contains the electric particles that produce the aurora, the green and red lights seen near the poles. It is also the home of the International Space Station, which orbits at about four hundred kilometres, and of many satellites. The layer expands and contracts as the sun's activity changes, and this affects the paths of satellites, which must be adjusted regularly.

The outermost layer is the exosphere, where the atmosphere fades into space. Here the gas is so thin that the particles rarely collide, and light atoms such as hydrogen and helium can escape from the Earth altogether. There is no sharp upper limit, but the exosphere is thought to extend to about ten thousand kilometres. Dr Ingrid Solberg, an atmospheric physicist, says that it is the most remote part of the planet, yet it is the first to meet the stream of particles which the sun throws out, and so it provides valuable warning of storms in space that can damage satellites and electrical networks.

Understanding the layers is not simply a matter of curiosity. Weather forecasts depend on the troposphere, radio communications depend on the electric particles above, and our safety on the ozone layer. Dr Solberg points out that human activity has altered the lowest layers, by adding gases that trap heat, but also the highest ones, since thousands of satellites and pieces of space rubbish now orbit the planet. She urges nations to cooperate in keeping the environment clean, from the ground to the edge of space, since the atmosphere, unlike a country, has no borders. A single volcanic eruption or industrial accident can send pollution thousands of kilometres from its source, and for this reason the problem can only be solved by agreement between many countries.
